questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the standard error for a replicated set of observations
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer replicates a star-count measurement 4 times and records a sample standard deviation of 6.0 counts; find the standard error of the mean.
questions.explanation: Divide the sample standard deviation by the square root of the replication count: 6.0 divided by 2 equals 3.0. A smaller replication count would inflate this error.
questions.hint: Divide standard deviation by square root of n.

questions.stem: Astronomer Aisha doubles her sample of galaxies while keeping the same confidence level; what happens to the margin of error for a proportion?

options.misconception: reverses the sample size effect on precision

options.text: It stays the same because confidence level is unchanged

questions.explanation: Full width is twice the margin of error, so 2 times 1.5 equals 3.0 magnitudes. The margin is only half the width.
questions.hint: Multiply the margin of error by two.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Independence and the five percent rule
questions.learningObjective: Compute sample fraction
questions.stem: Astronomer Carlos samples 24 stars without replacement from 300; what is the sample fraction of the population?
questions.explanation: The sample fraction is 24 divided by 300, or 0.08. That exceeds 0.05, so independence is not well approximated.
questions.hint: Divide sample size by population size.

questions.stem: Astronomer Fiona has 100 nights with standard deviation 10.0 arcseconds; compute the standard error of the mean.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute required sample size
questions.stem: Astronomer George wants a standard error of 1.0 with population standard deviation 5.0; how many observations does he need?
questions.explanation: Set 5.0 over square root of n equal to 1.0, so square root of n equals 5, and n equals 25. He needs 25 observations.
questions.hint: Solve 5 divided by square root of n equals 1.

questions.stem: Astronomer Hannah surveys 100 amateurs and finds 30 percent own a telescope; approximate the margin of error at 95 percent confidence.

It stays the same because confidence is fixed

options.misconception: reverses the sample size effect on width

options.text: It becomes zero with a large sample

questions.learningObjective: Compute maximum sample size
questions.stem: Astronomer Kate's population has 800 stars; what is the maximum sample size satisfying the five percent rule?
questions.explanation: Five percent of 800 is 40, so the sample must be no more than 40. This keeps sampling without replacement close to independent.
questions.hint: Take five percent of 800.
